Lexical search excels at exact identifiers, product codes, names, and rare terms. Semantic search handles paraphrase and conceptual similarity. Hybrid retrieval collects candidates from both and fuses their ranks before optional reranking.
Raw lexical and vector scores live on different scales; rank fusion avoids pretending they are directly comparable without calibration.

challenge.instructions: Users search both exact error code E1042 and natural-language descriptions. Choose the strongest design.

choices.text: Retrieve lexical and vector candidates, fuse ranks, then rerank the combined set.
Use vectors only and discard exact codes.
Use character count as the only rank signal.

challenge.explanation: Lexical retrieval preserves exact identifiers while vector retrieval catches paraphrases; fusion uses their complementary strengths.
hints: One query type is exact; the other is semantic.
Preserve candidates from both signals.

lessons.title: Evaluate Retrieval before Generation
lessons.summary: Measure whether known relevant sources are present in the candidate set.

contentBlocks.text: Retrieval needs its own ground truth

For labeled queries, recall@k measures the share of relevant documents appearing in the top k. Mean reciprocal rank rewards placing the first relevant result early. Slice results by query type, language, and source freshness to uncover uneven behavior.
If the needed evidence is absent, generation cannot cite it reliably. Diagnose retrieval separately from answer generation.

challenge.instructions: A query has two known relevant documents; the top three results contain one. What is recall@3?
challenge.explanation: One of two relevant documents was retrieved, so recall is 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5.
hints: Count retrieved relevant items.
Divide by all known relevant items.

courses.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
courses.summary: Build grounded answer systems from document ingestion through retrieval, citations, abstention, and component-level evaluation.

modules.title: Ingest and Retrieve Evidence
modules.summary: Transform source documents into traceable chunks and retrieve evidence suited to the user’s question.

lessons.title: Ground Answers in Retrieved Evidence
lessons.summary: Understand RAG as an evidence pipeline rather than a way to retrain model knowledge.

contentBlocks.text: Retrieve first, generate second

RAG searches an external collection at request time and places selected passages into model context. It is useful for private, changing, or source-cited knowledge because documents can be updated independently of model weights.
The grounded loop

challenge.instructions: Explain why a policy assistant should retrieve the current handbook rather than rely only on model pretraining.
challenge.explanation: Retrieval supplies the latest controlled source at request time and makes citations possible; pretrained knowledge may be old, absent, or impossible to audit.
hints: Policy versions change after model training.
The answer should point back to an authoritative source.

lessons.title: Chunk around Meaningful Units
lessons.summary: Balance retrievability, self-contained meaning, and context efficiency when splitting documents.

contentBlocks.text: A chunk is the unit the retriever can find

Chunks that are too large mix unrelated topics and waste context. Chunks that are too small lose definitions and qualifications. Prefer headings, paragraphs, procedures, and table rows as semantic boundaries, then test sizes on real questions.
Overlap can preserve sentences crossing a boundary, but excessive overlap duplicates results and crowds the context with near-copies.

challenge.instructions: A five-step incident procedure has warnings attached to steps 2 and 4. Which chunking rule is strongest?

choices.text: Keep each procedure section with its steps and associated warnings.
Split every fixed 20 characters regardless of sentence boundaries.
Put the entire handbook in one chunk.

challenge.explanation: Semantic sections preserve the relationship between actions and warnings while remaining focused enough to retrieve.
hints: A retrieved chunk should make sense on its own.
Do not separate a warning from the step it qualifies.

lessons.title: Create Overlapping Word Chunks
lessons.summary: Implement a transparent chunker with validated size and overlap invariants.

contentBlocks.text: Advance by size minus overlap

A simple word chunker is not production-grade semantic parsing, but it makes the mechanics visible. The step must be positive, so overlap must be smaller than chunk size; the final slice naturally contains fewer words.

challenge.instructions: Validate overlap, advance by chunk_size - overlap, and join each slice into text.
challenge.explanation: The positive step controls repeated boundary words, and slicing safely handles the shorter final chunk.
hints: Step is chunk_size minus overlap.
Slice words from start through start + chunk_size.

lessons.title: Filter with Trustworthy Metadata
lessons.summary: Use access, version, language, and time filters before similarity ranking.

contentBlocks.text: Similarity cannot enforce authorization

Metadata narrows search to documents the requester may access and that fit the task. Tenant ID and permissions should be derived from authenticated server context, never from user-supplied prompt text.
Useful chunk metadata

challenge.instructions: A shared index stores documents for many companies. Choose the safe query design.

choices.text: Apply an authenticated tenant filter inside retrieval before candidates are returned.
Retrieve globally and ask the model not to quote other tenants.
Let the user type any tenant ID into the question.

challenge.explanation: The retrieval layer must prevent unauthorized documents from entering context at all; model instructions are not an access-control boundary.
hints: Unauthorized evidence should never reach the model.
Trust identity from authentication, not prompt text.

lessons.title: Rewrite Follow-Ups for Retrieval
lessons.summary: Create a standalone search query from a short follow-up and known conversation subject.

contentBlocks.text: Search needs the referent, not the pronoun

A follow-up such as "when does it expire?" is meaningful in conversation but poor for search. Query rewriting resolves references using bounded history while preserving the user’s intent; it should not invent new constraints or facts.
Log both original and rewritten queries. Evaluation must catch rewrites that silently change the question.

challenge.instructions: If a subject is known, prefix it to the stripped follow-up; otherwise return the follow-up unchanged.
challenge.explanation: The known subject supplies missing retrieval context while the original question remains intact.
hints: Check that subject exists and is not whitespace.
Return question unchanged without a subject.

modules.title: Generate, Cite, and Evaluate
modules.summary: Assemble evidence into a controlled answer contract and diagnose failures by component.

lessons.title: Assemble Evidence, Not a Document Dump
lessons.summary: Order, deduplicate, label, and budget retrieved passages before generation.

contentBlocks.text: Context assembly is the bridge to generation

Retrieve broadly enough for recall, then rerank, deduplicate overlapping chunks, and include source labels. Order passages by relevance or a task-specific sequence while reserving answer tokens and preserving qualifications.
An evidence packet should expose

challenge.instructions: Explain why five nearly identical overlapping chunks may hurt even when all are relevant.
challenge.explanation: They consume scarce context, overrepresent one source, and can crowd out complementary evidence needed for a complete answer.
hints: Count unique information, not just relevant chunks.
Repeated evidence changes the balance of context.

lessons.title: Make Citations Verifiable
lessons.summary: Attach claims to stable source references rather than trusting model-generated link text.

contentBlocks.text: Citation generation needs source control

Give each retrieved passage an application-assigned source ID and instruct the model to cite only those IDs. After generation, verify every cited ID exists and render the final title and URL from trusted metadata rather than model-written links.
Citation presence is not citation correctness. Evaluate whether the cited passage actually supports the nearby claim.

challenge.instructions: The model returns [S3]. Where should the displayed URL come from?

choices.text: Trusted metadata stored for retrieved source S3.
Any URL the model invents after the answer.
The user’s unverified prompt instructions.

challenge.explanation: Application metadata binds the allowed source ID to an authoritative URL and prevents fabricated links.
hints: The model should select an ID, not author trust metadata.
Verify the ID was in the request context.

lessons.title: Build a Citation-Constrained Prompt
lessons.summary: Render numbered sources and require grounded answers or explicit abstention.

contentBlocks.text: Abstention is part of the output contract

The prompt should permit an "insufficient evidence" response when sources do not support the question. Otherwise the model is pressured to complete an answer from prior knowledge or plausible invention.

Answer only from SOURCES. Cite source IDs after claims.
If the sources are insufficient, say: INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE.

challenge.instructions: Create [id] text lines, then append the question and abstention instruction.
challenge.solution:
def rag_prompt(question, sources):
    lines = []
    for source in sources:
        source_line = f"[{source['id']}] {source['text']}"
        lines.append(source_line)
    evidence = "\n".join(lines)
    rule = "Use only SOURCES and cite IDs. If insufficient, say INSUFFICIENT_EVIDENCE."
    return f"{rule}\nSOURCES:\n{evidence}\nQUESTION: {question}"

testCases.expected: empty SOURCES section with abstention rule

challenge.explanation: Application-owned IDs make citations checkable, while the explicit insufficient-evidence path prevents forced guessing.
hints: Format each line as [id] text.
Include the rule before evidence and the question after it.

lessons.title: Route RAG Failures to the Right Layer
lessons.summary: Separate corpus, retrieval, reranking, context, and generation defects before choosing a fix.

contentBlocks.text: Inspect the evidence funnel

When an answer fails, first ask whether authoritative content exists in the corpus, then whether it appeared in candidates, survived reranking, fit the final context, and was used faithfully. Changing the generation prompt cannot repair a missing source document.
Failure labels

challenge.instructions: The correct passage exists and ranks second, but it is removed when only the top one chunk is sent. What should change first?

choices.text: Context-selection policy or final chunk count.
Re-collect the source document.
Train a tokenizer from scratch.

challenge.explanation: Retrieval found the evidence; the loss happens at final context assembly, so that stage is the direct repair target.
hints: Locate the last stage where the passage is present.
Fix the first stage that drops necessary evidence.

lessons.title: Evaluate Retrieval and Answers Separately
lessons.summary: Combine retrieval recall, answer correctness, faithfulness, citation support, and abstention quality.

contentBlocks.text: One end-to-end score hides the repair

A RAG evaluation set should include questions, relevant sources, expected answer facts, and unanswerable cases. Measure candidate recall and ranking separately from answer correctness, evidence faithfulness, citation support, and appropriate abstention.
Include time-sensitive and access-controlled cases so evaluation covers freshness and authorization, not only semantic relevance.

challenge.prompt: Interpret a faithful but incomplete answer
challenge.instructions: Every answer claim is supported, but half the required facts are absent because retrieval missed a document. Which component is the first suspect?

choices.text: Retrieval recall
Citation formatting color
The arithmetic in softmax

challenge.explanation: Faithfulness is good for the supplied evidence, but missing required source facts points to corpus or retrieval recall before generation.
hints: The model did not invent unsupported content.
Ask whether all necessary evidence reached it.

courses.title: LLM Application Architecture
courses.summary: Wrap probabilistic models in typed contracts, gateways, retries, queues, budgets, state, and observable application flows.

modules.title: Typed Contracts and the Model Gateway
modules.summary: Keep business invariants deterministic while centralizing model access and failure handling.

lessons.title: Use a Deterministic Shell
lessons.summary: Place language understanding inside code-enforced authorization, validation, and persistence boundaries.

contentBlocks.text: The model proposes; trusted code disposes

Models are useful for ambiguity, interpretation, and synthesis. Deterministic services should own identity, permissions, prices, quotas, state transitions, and irreversible actions. Treat model output as untrusted input to the next layer.
A safe request path

challenge.instructions: A model suggests refund amounts, but automatic refunds cannot exceed €50. Explain where the cap belongs.
challenge.explanation: The refund service must enforce the cap before any transaction; a prompt may describe the rule but cannot provide the hard guarantee.
hints: Ask which layer controls the actual transfer.
Model output is a proposal, not authorization.

lessons.title: Constrain Output before Parsing
lessons.summary: Use schema-native generation, typed parsing, and domain validation as separate gates.

contentBlocks.text: Valid syntax can still express an invalid action

A schema can require fields and types, greatly reducing malformed output. After parsing, domain checks must still enforce ranges, cross-field relationships, references, and permissions before anything downstream acts.
Preserve raw response, parsed object, validation result, and schema version in traces so failures are diagnosable.

challenge.instructions: The model returns valid JSON with {"discount_percent": 900}. What should the application do?

choices.text: Reject it with domain-range validation before execution.
Apply it because the JSON parsed.
Hide the value in logs and continue.

challenge.explanation: Schema syntax does not establish business validity; a 900% discount violates a range invariant and must be rejected.
hints: Parsing answers "is it shaped correctly?" only.
A business rule answers "is this allowed?"

lessons.title: Validate a Model Proposal
lessons.summary: Convert typed output into either an accepted domain object or explicit validation errors.

contentBlocks.text: Make rejected states observable
A validator should collect precise reasons rather than returning a vague false. Error codes support retries, monitoring, and human review while keeping policy logic outside prompt text.

challenge.instructions: Return error codes when amount is negative, exceeds the limit, or reason is blank.
challenge.starterCode:
def validate_refund(proposal, limit):
    errors = []
    amount = proposal["amount"]
    if amount < 0:
        errors.append("negative_amount")
    ____
    ____
    return errors
challenge.explanation: Independent checks preserve every violated invariant, producing useful feedback without trusting the model to self-police.
hints: Compare amount > limit.
Get reason with an empty fallback and strip whitespace.

lessons.title: Centralize Providers behind a Gateway
lessons.summary: Create one internal interface for provider calls, policy, telemetry, and controlled fallback.

contentBlocks.text: Applications should depend on capabilities, not vendor payloads

A model gateway translates an internal request contract into provider-specific APIs. It centralizes authentication, model allowlists, timeouts, retries, rate limits, logging, redaction, cost attribution, and feature compatibility.
Avoid a lowest-common-denominator abstraction: expose capabilities such as structured output, tools, vision, and streaming explicitly and reject unsupported combinations.

challenge.instructions: The primary model times out during a schema-extraction request. Choose a safe fallback policy.

choices.text: Fallback only to an approved model supporting the same schema contract, then revalidate output.
Use any available text model and skip validation.
Retry forever without a deadline.

challenge.explanation: Fallback must preserve required capabilities and output guarantees; validation remains necessary regardless of provider.
hints: Feature compatibility is part of the contract.
Fallback changes the model, not the business rules.

lessons.title: Retry Only Transient Failures
lessons.summary: Classify retryable statuses and calculate bounded exponential backoff with jitter-ready structure.

contentBlocks.text: Retries consume time, money, and capacity

Rate limits, timeouts, and temporary server failures may recover. Invalid requests, failed authorization, and impossible schema constraints usually will not. Bound attempts by a request deadline and make consequential operations idempotent before retrying.

delay = min(base_delay * (2 ** attempt), max_delay)
# Add small random jitter in production.

challenge.instructions: Retry 429 and 5xx statuses, and return capped exponential delay; otherwise return None.
challenge.solution:
def retry_delay(status, attempt, base=0.5, maximum=8.0):
    retryable = status == 429 or status >= 500
    if not retryable:
        return None
    exponential_delay = base * (2 ** attempt)
    delay = min(exponential_delay, maximum)
    return delay
challenge.explanation: Only transient status classes receive backoff, and the maximum prevents waits from growing without bound.
hints: Compute base * 2 raised to attempt.
Use min with maximum and return the result.

modules.title: Runtime Flow, State, and Budgets
modules.summary: Choose synchronous, streamed, or queued execution and protect the system under load.

lessons.title: Synchronous, Streaming, and Asynchronous Work
lessons.summary: Match the user experience and failure model to the duration and interactivity of a task.

contentBlocks.text: Execution mode is a product decision

A short classification can complete synchronously. Streaming improves perceived latency for an answer consumed as it arrives. Long document jobs should enter a durable queue with status, cancellation, retries, and stored results so they survive client disconnects.
Streaming changes delivery, not correctness. Validate the completed structured result before executing downstream actions.

challenge.instructions: A report analyzes 500 documents and may take ten minutes. Explain the appropriate pattern.
challenge.explanation: Submit a durable asynchronous job, return a job ID, expose progress and cancellation, checkpoint work, and notify or let the client poll for the stored result.
hints: The client connection may not stay open ten minutes.
The work should survive process and network interruptions.

lessons.title: Protect Capacity with Backpressure
lessons.summary: Limit in-flight work and queue growth before overload becomes cascading failure.

contentBlocks.text: Unlimited queues convert overload into delayed failure

Concurrency limits bound expensive model calls. Bounded queues reject, defer, or degrade excess traffic instead of consuming all memory and waiting beyond useful deadlines. Per-tenant quotas prevent one customer from exhausting shared capacity.
Overload controls

challenge.instructions: All workers are busy and queued jobs already exceed their useful deadline. What is the safest behavior?

choices.text: Reject or defer new work with a clear retry signal rather than growing the queue.
Accept unlimited work until the process crashes.
Hide queue delay from clients.

challenge.explanation: Backpressure preserves system recovery and gives callers actionable information instead of accepting work that cannot succeed on time.
hints: A queued request can become useless before execution.
Bound memory and time, not only worker count.

lessons.title: Route Requests within a Budget
lessons.summary: Select the least costly approved model that satisfies capability and token requirements.

contentBlocks.text: Model choice can be a policy function

A router should filter candidates by required capabilities and context size before comparing price or latency. Recording the decision reason makes cost changes explainable and supports offline replay against production traffic.

eligible = [m for m in models if required <= set(m["capabilities"]) and tokens <= m["context"]]
return min(eligible, key=lambda m: m["cost"])

challenge.instructions: Filter by required capability and sufficient context, then return the lowest-cost model name or None.
challenge.explanation: Capability and context are hard constraints; cost optimizes only among candidates that can actually perform the task.
hints: Require supports and fits together.
Use min with model cost as the key.

lessons.title: Separate Conversation and Business State
lessons.summary: Keep chat history, workflow state, and system-of-record data under different consistency rules.

contentBlocks.text: A transcript is not a database transaction

Conversation state supports linguistic continuity and can be summarized or pruned. Business state—orders, approvals, balances—must live in authoritative services with versioning and concurrency control. The model receives a snapshot and requests actions through validated commands.
Use idempotency keys for retried actions and optimistic version checks when a proposal depends on state that may have changed.

challenge.instructions: The model saw five items in stock, but inventory may change before purchase. Choose the correct boundary.

choices.text: The inventory service rechecks stock and state version when executing the requested purchase.
The model’s earlier context becomes the permanent source of truth.
Skip concurrency checks because the assistant sounded confident.

challenge.explanation: Authoritative state must be checked at execution time; model context is a potentially stale snapshot.
hints: State can change after prompt construction.
Execution belongs to the service that owns inventory.

lessons.title: Trace a Production Request End to End
lessons.summary: Place authentication, retrieval, model calls, validation, execution, and telemetry in a defensible order.

contentBlocks.text: Reliability emerges from the whole path

A production request crosses trust and failure boundaries. Authenticate first, establish a deadline and trace, load authorized context, call the gateway, parse and validate output, execute idempotently if allowed, and record outcome metrics without leaking sensitive content.
Observability spans every boundary

challenge.instructions: For a tool-using assistant, which must happen before the external action executes?

choices.text: Validate tool arguments and recheck authorization in deterministic code.
Execute first, then see whether the arguments were allowed.
Trust the model because its output matched JSON syntax.

challenge.explanation: Typed parsing is only the first gate; semantic validation and current authorization must precede consequential side effects.
hints: The action may be irreversible.
The model proposal is untrusted input to the tool layer.
